item.title: Community Concert: Nu-Blu — Thu Nov 5, 12:00 AM
item.description:
The Morgan County Community Concerts Association presents Nu-Blu on Thursday, November 5, at 7 pm at Hoosier Harvest Church in Martinsville. North Carolina-based Nu-Blu, has quickly established themselves as one of the top acoustic acts in the music industry. Led by husband and wife, Daniel \(guitar, vocals\) and Carolyn Routh \(bass, vocals\), Austin Hefflefinger on banjo, and Justin Harrison on mandolin, Nu-Blu delivers a warm, layered Appalachian sound. Blending seamless vocal harmonies, they deliver upbeat, blazing-fingers pick work as well as gentle, heartwarming ballads, all with a natural togetherness that can’t be faked, creating a connection with your audience and variety to suit fans of any music genre. The Morgan County Community Concerts Association presents several concerts each year in Morgan County, with performances taking place at area high school auditoriums. Attendees can subscribe to the entire series, or purchase single show performances.
Source: Limestone Post, V

item.title: Micro-mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature — Thu Nov 5 — LILLY LIBRARY
item.description: "Myths are the world's dreams."- Joseph Campbell.To believe is to be human.One of the greatest forces known to humankind,belief is a universal impetus, one that has raised and toppled temples, instigated and eased wars, and inspired written works, both monumental and miniature. This exhibition showcases a selection of minute materials that pertain to mythologies and belief systems from across the world. From ancient Mesopotamian myth to modern Native American spirituality, belief transcends time and history and intertwines human existence within our world.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is a miniature book exhibition which seeks to highlight some of our oldest and most powerful stories, as well as those who preserved them.Mythological influence has shaped the world around us. Whether that be through architecture, art, or literature, myths serve as a testament to human cultural memory and the preservation of intangible tradition. Myths pull back the curtain of the past

item.title: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, the Moment — Thu Nov 5 — LILLY LIBRARY
item.description: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Momentexamines a crucial time in American history through the collections of the Lilly Library. The first printing of the Declaration of Independence, one of only twenty-six copies known today, is the centerpiece of the exhibition. Printed immediately for distribution, it is the source of all revolutionary era reprintings. The famous hand-written version was an official formality created later, signed in August, and stored away.Books, pamphlets, newspapers, prints, and letters allow viewers to explore key questions about this moment in time. How did a people proud to be in the British empire come to believe independence was possible or even desirable? What ideas and historical events did they draw on to justify resistance to Great Britain? What kinds of communication networks would be crucial for circulating the Declaration and countless other revolutionary documents throughout the colonies?This exhibition is part of America 250 at IU (

item.title: The Declaration of Independence: The Signers — Thu Nov 5 — LILLY LIBRARY
item.description: IU Libraries Lilly Library invites you to The Declaration of Independence: The Signers, an exhibition of letters and documents bearing the autographs of the fifty-six men who signed the August 2, 1776 handwritten copy of the Declaration. Though the length and content of these letters and documents vary widely, from brief notes or orders to long and detailed personal letters, they all offer insight into the daily lives, activities, and concerns of the signers. One aspect of their lives that these documents don't reveal, however, is the ownership of slaves by a great many of the signers, which is discussed in the "Race, Slavery, and Native Americans" section of the exhibition in the Lilly Library's North Gallery, The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment. (https://libraries.indiana.edu/lilly-library/declaration-independence) Documents signed by fifty-four of the fifty-six signers are displayed in the Lilly Library's South Gallery. Documents signed by the two other signers

item.title: Aanikoobijigan (Ancestor / Great-Grandparent / Great-Grandchild) Film Screening — Sat Nov 7, 1:00 PM — IU CINEMA
item.description: "What's the difference between an archaeologist and a grave robber?" an elder asks. "A degree," he laughs. Aanikoobijigan examines the ongoing struggle to repatriate indigenous ancestors' remains from museums and archives, exposing the thin line between archaeology and grave robbery. With striking visuals and grounded indigenous perspectives, Aanikoobijigan challenges institutional resistance to decolonization and affirms that returning ancestors to the earth restores memory, dignity, and balance, reminding us that no community can be whole until their ancestors are finally laid to rest. The film's directors, Adam and Zack Khalil, were recently named among the cohort of Filmmaker Magazine's 25 New Film Faces to Watch. [80 min; documentary; English and Anishinaabemowin with English subtitles]The screening will be followed by a conversation betweenIU Indianapolis professor Dr. Holly Cusack-McVeigh, Anthropology and Museum Studies and Public Scholar of Collections and Community Curation,

item.title: Acoustic Colonialism: Between Attentive Listening and Indigenous Interference — Sat Nov 7, 8:00 PM — INDIANA MEMORIAL UNION (UNION BUILDING)
item.description:
This talk will offer an author's view on the key theoretical, methodological, and historical concepts that form part of his book, Acoustic Colonialism: Acts of Mapuche Interference (Duke UP, 2025). Theorizations regarding what the author calls "acoustic colonialism", "the colonial ear", and "indigenous interference" reverberate throughout his book, including the Mapuche notion of allkütun (attentive listening). Cárcamo-Huechante elaborates on these concepts in the context of Ngülü Mapu–or what is currently known as central and southern Chile, part of the broader Mapuche territory (Wallmapu).
Source: IU First Nations Center

item.description: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Momentexamines a crucial time in American history through the collections of the Lilly Library. The first printing of the Declaration of Independence, one of only twenty-six copies known today, is the centerpiece of the exhibition. Printed immediately for distribution, it is the source of all revolutionary era reprintings. The famous hand-written version was an official formality created later, signed in August, and stored away.Books, pamphlets, newspapers, prints, and letters allow viewers to explore key questions about this moment in time. How did a people proud to be in the British empire come to believe independence was possible or even desirable? What ideas and historical events did they draw on to justify resistance to Great Britain? What kinds of communication networks would be crucial for circulating the Declaration and countless other revolutionary documents throughout the colonies?This exhibition is part of America 250 at IU (

item.description: IU Libraries Lilly Library invites you to The Declaration of Independence: The Signers, an exhibition of letters and documents bearing the autographs of the fifty-six men who signed the August 2, 1776 handwritten copy of the Declaration. Though the length and content of these letters and documents vary widely, from brief notes or orders to long and detailed personal letters, they all offer insight into the daily lives, activities, and concerns of the signers. One aspect of their lives that these documents don't reveal, however, is the ownership of slaves by a great many of the signers, which is discussed in the "Race, Slavery, and Native Americans" section of the exhibition in the Lilly Library's North Gallery, The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment. item.title: Panel discussion with Professors of European background — Thu Nov 12, 6:30 PM — IMU Oak Room
item.description:
Studying & Working Abroad: A Faculty Panel What does an international academic and professional career actually look like? Join EBA for an evening with three Kelley professors whose careers have crossed borders.
Professor Sridhar Arcot went from the London School of Economics to fifteen years at ESSEC in Paris, where he was Academic Director of the MSc in Finance. He now co-directs Kelley’s Capital Markets & Banking Workshop. Professor Francesco Marchionne built his academic and professional career across Ancona, Turin and Nottingham before coming to Bloomington. His class trips to Italy have inspired many students to study abroad. Professor Andreas Hauskrecht started at Freie Universität Berlin and has spent more than three decades advising Vietnam’s government and central bank. He has also advised central banks in Bolivia, Ecuador, Laos and Moldova.
We’ll talk about choosing between European and US programs, building a career that spans countries, and how to make a semester or job
